In summary, our research is concerned with
the search for the dark matter in the Universe and the study of the fundamental nature of the interactions between dark matter and normal matter, which are still unknown.
the detection of dark matter, the nature of which is still unknown.
a search for the existence of weakly interacting, massive particles (WIMPs), which are candidates to explain the dark matter in the universe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SIMPLE experiment has not observed any evidence for WIMPs, but it has significantly reduced the allowed regions of the parameter space.
the SIMPLE experiment has excluded all of the allowed region of phase space previously defined by XENOS, CDMS, DAMA, EDELWEISS, and ZEPLIN.
the SIMPLE Phase II experiment has excluded the entire parameter space of weakly interacting dark matter for masses above 45 GeV/c⁻².
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have excluded the possibility of a dark matter signal in the SIMPLE experiment at a level of 2.5σ.
we have now excluded the possibility that a dark matter candidate, with a mass in the range of 10-100 GeV/c², could be the sole source of the galactic halo dark matter.
the SIMPLE experiment, together with other experiments, has significantly improved the sensitivity to WIMPs in both the spin-dependent and the spin-independent sectors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spin-dependent interaction of weakly interacting dark matter particles with nuclei is not favored by the data.

we have demonstrated that a superheated droplets detector array can be operated in an environment with a high level of neutron background and that the detector can be operated with a low threshold, thus allowing the search for low mass WIMPs.
the spin-dependent interaction is not required for a WIMP interpretation of our data.
